primary_claim: Importance-sampling methods (ITGIS, MHIS) for estimating low-probability single-token language model outputs outperform activation-extrapolation methods (QLD, GLD), and both outperform naive sampling, when estimating ground-truth probabilities between 1e-9 and 1e-5 across 8 input distributions and 3 model sizes (1/2/4-layer transformers) under a fixed budget of roughly 65,000 forward passes.

effect.metric: Itakura-Saito loss of probability estimates, averaged across 8 distributions and 3 model sizes
effect.value: both importance-sampling methods (ITGIS, MHIS) outperform Quadratic Logit Decomposition, which outperforms Gaussian Logit Difference (barely better than an optimal constant, i.e. naive sampling); ITGIS does better on smaller models, MHIS does better on larger models

contradicts_or_qualifies: Notes theoretical cases (e.g. estimating the probability of a particular SHA-256 hash output) where importance sampling would perform worse than activation-extrapolation-style methods, despite importance sampling outperforming activation extrapolation in this paper's empirical setting
stated_future_work: Extend the empirical setup to non-independent (correlated-token) input distributions
Extend to output behaviors involving more than a single token
Develop more accurate estimation methods, e.g. inspired by layer-by-layer activation modeling
Define the input distribution as the output of a separate generative model and adapt current estimation methods (GLD and QLD are noted as input-agnostic and directly applicable)
limitations_stated: Only input distributions that factor into independent tokens were used, which is necessary for ITGIS's definition and convenient for MHIS's efficient sampling

Only single-token behaviors sampled at temperature 0 were studied, which is unrealistic since single-token outputs could easily be blocked with a filter; behaviors of actual concern likely involve long autoregressive chains or interaction with the external world
quote: We find that the methods based on importance sampling outperform methods based on activation extrapolation, though both outperform naive sampling.
